title: Mental Health — Suicide Risk II: Assessment, Precautions & Priority Care (Set 21)
subtitle: Phase-2 depth: risk stratification and lethality of a plan, matching level of observation (1:1 vs close checks), means restriction specifics, warning signs of imminent risk, protective factors, safety planning vs 'no-suicide contracts,' responding to an attempt on the unit, high-risk transitions, and prioritization
scenario: Applying suicide-risk assessment and safety care in real situations: judging which client is at highest risk, choosing the right level of observation, restricting means, recognizing imminent-risk cues, responding to an attempt, and keeping the client safe through high-risk transitions.

steps.q: Which client is at the HIGHEST acute risk for suicide and needs the most immediate protection?

opts.text: A client with a specific plan, an available lethal means, a prior attempt, and who is giving away belongings
opts.rat: A specific plan plus available means, a history of attempts, and imminent-risk behaviors (giving away possessions) together indicate the highest acute risk.

opts.text: A client who says life is stressful but denies any thoughts of self-harm and has strong support
opts.rat: Stress without suicidal thoughts and with support is much lower acute risk.

opts.text: A client with vague sadness, no plan, and future-oriented goals
opts.rat: No plan and future orientation indicate lower acute risk.

opts.text: A client who is grieving but engaged in treatment and denies self-harm
opts.rat: Grief with engagement and denial of self-harm is lower acute risk than an active plan with means.

steps.q: When assessing the lethality of a client's suicidal plan, which factor suggests HIGHER risk?

opts.text: A specific, detailed plan using a highly lethal and readily available method
opts.rat: Specificity, high lethality of method, and easy access to the means all raise the danger of the plan.

opts.text: A vague thought with no method in mind
opts.rat: A vague thought without a method is lower risk than a specific, feasible plan.

opts.text: No access to any means
opts.rat: Lack of access to means lowers immediate risk.

opts.text: An unclear, far-off idea with no timeframe
opts.rat: A far-off, unclear idea is lower risk than a specific, imminent plan.

steps.q: As part of means restriction for a client at risk, the technician should ensure the environment is cleared of items such as:

opts.text: Sharps, cords/belts/shoelaces, glass, plastic bags, and access to medications
opts.rat: Removing or securing items that could be used for self-harm (sharps, ligature risks, glass, bags, medications) is central to a safe environment.

opts.text: Books and family photographs
opts.rat: These are not means of self-harm and support comfort, not risk.

opts.text: The client's eyeglasses needed to see
opts.rat: Removing needed assistive items is not the goal; the focus is items usable for self-harm, per assessment/policy.

opts.text: Healthy snacks
opts.rat: Snacks are not a self-harm means; means restriction targets dangerous items.

steps.q: A client with active suicidal ideation and a plan is admitted. The MOST appropriate level of observation is:

opts.text: Continuous one-to-one observation with constant visual contact at all times
opts.rat: Active ideation with a plan warrants continuous 1:1 observation so the client is never out of the staff member's sight.

opts.text: A check every few hours
opts.rat: Intermittent checks are inadequate for a client with an active plan.

opts.text: No special observation
opts.rat: A client with an active plan requires close, continuous observation.

opts.text: Observation only during the day shift
opts.rat: Risk does not stop at night; observation is continuous as ordered.

steps.q: While providing one-to-one suicide observation, the technician must:

opts.text: Keep the client within sight at all times—including during toileting/showering per policy—and hand off to another staff member before ever stepping away
opts.rat: Constant visual observation means never leaving the client unwatched, even briefly; coverage is handed off directly to another staff member.

opts.text: Step out for a few minutes when the client seems calm
opts.rat: Leaving—even briefly—breaks the constant observation that keeps the client safe.

opts.text: Watch the client only from the hallway camera
opts.rat: 1:1 requires direct, in-person constant observation, not remote monitoring alone.

opts.text: Allow the client full privacy in the bathroom
opts.rat: For a client on 1:1, observation continues in the bathroom per policy because that is a high-risk location.

steps.q: Which cluster suggests IMMINENT suicide risk and should prompt immediate action?

opts.text: Giving away prized possessions, saying goodbye, putting affairs in order, and sudden calm after deep despair
opts.rat: These behaviors can signal that a client has decided to act and require immediate protective response.

opts.text: Making concrete plans for a vacation next year
opts.rat: Future-oriented planning suggests lower imminent risk.

opts.text: Engaging actively in therapy and setting goals
opts.rat: Active engagement and goal-setting are protective signs.

opts.text: Asking about discharge follow-up appointments
opts.rat: Planning for follow-up reflects future orientation, not imminent risk.

steps.q: Which is a PROTECTIVE factor that may lower a client's suicide risk?

opts.text: Strong social support, reasons for living, and future-oriented plans
opts.rat: Connectedness, reasons for living, and hope for the future are recognized protective factors—though they never remove the need for indicated precautions.

opts.text: Social isolation and hopelessness
opts.rat: These are risk factors, not protective factors.

opts.text: Easy access to lethal means
opts.rat: Access to means increases risk.

opts.text: A recent major loss with no support
opts.rat: Loss without support raises risk.

steps.q: Regarding a signed 'no-suicide contract' (a client's written promise not to harm themselves), the technician should understand that it:

opts.text: Does NOT guarantee safety; collaborative safety planning and appropriate precautions are what protect the client
opts.rat: A contract cannot prevent suicide; ongoing risk assessment, safety planning, means restriction, and observation are the real safeguards.

opts.text: Guarantees the client will not attempt suicide
opts.rat: No contract can guarantee safety; it is not a substitute for precautions.

opts.text: Removes the need for any observation
opts.rat: Precautions and observation remain necessary regardless of a contract.

opts.text: Is a legally binding safety device
opts.rat: It is not a reliable safety device; safety planning and monitoring protect the client.

steps.q: A client on the unit is found having just attempted self-harm and is injured. The technician's FIRST priority is to:

opts.text: Ensure immediate physical safety—address the injury/airway and call for help
opts.rat: Life-threatening physical needs (airway, bleeding, injury) come first, along with summoning emergency help.

opts.text: Document the event in detail before doing anything else
opts.rat: Documentation follows once the client is physically safe; care comes first.

opts.text: Leave to notify the family right away
opts.rat: The client's immediate physical safety and getting help take priority over notifications.

opts.text: Lecture the client about their behavior
opts.rat: This is unhelpful and unsafe; immediate physical care is the priority.

steps.q: After a client has attempted self-harm and is medically stabilized, the technician should recognize that:

opts.text: Risk remains high; close observation should be maintained and not relaxed prematurely
opts.rat: The period following an attempt carries continued high risk, so protective observation is maintained rather than reduced too soon.

opts.text: The client is now safe and precautions can be stopped
opts.rat: Risk does not end with medical stabilization; precautions continue.

opts.text: Observation can be reduced immediately to save staff time
opts.rat: Reducing observation prematurely is dangerous after an attempt.

opts.text: The attempt means the client no longer wishes to die
opts.rat: An attempt does not resolve risk; continued protection and assessment are needed.

steps.q: Which period is recognized as a time of ELEVATED suicide risk requiring careful safety planning?

opts.text: Transitions such as after discharge or when precautions are being reduced
opts.rat: Transitions—especially the period after hospitalization or when observation is lowered—are recognized high-risk times needing follow-up and a safety plan.

opts.text: Only the moment of admission and no other time
opts.rat: Risk is not limited to admission; transitions like discharge are especially high-risk.

opts.text: Times when the client is closely supervised
opts.rat: Close supervision lowers immediate opportunity; reduced supervision and transitions raise risk.

opts.text: There is no period of elevated risk
opts.rat: Certain periods, like post-discharge, carry elevated risk.

steps.q: A client who has been severely depressed and hopeless suddenly appears calm, peaceful, and 'at peace.' The technician should:

opts.text: Reassess carefully and maintain precautions, because sudden calm can mean the client has decided to act on a suicide plan
opts.rat: An abrupt shift from despair to calm can indicate a resolved decision to die; precautions are maintained and the change is reported.

opts.text: Assume the client is cured and remove all precautions
opts.rat: Sudden calm is a warning sign, not proof of recovery; precautions continue.

opts.text: Reduce observation as a reward for improvement
opts.rat: Reducing observation on this cue can be dangerous.

opts.text: Ignore the change since the client seems better
opts.rat: The change is significant and must be assessed and reported, not ignored.

steps.q: A client confides a specific suicide plan and begs the technician, 'Please don't tell anyone.' The technician should:

opts.text: Explain that safety comes first and the team must be told, stay with the client, and report immediately
opts.rat: Client safety overrides a request for secrecy; the technician cannot keep it confidential, stays with the client, and reports at once.

opts.text: Promise to keep the plan secret
opts.rat: Promising secrecy about a suicide plan endangers the client and cannot be done.

opts.text: Agree and say nothing to the team
opts.rat: Withholding a disclosed plan is dangerous and violates safety duty.

opts.text: Leave the client alone to think it over
opts.rat: The client should not be left alone; stay and get help.

steps.q: On admission of a client at risk for suicide, an important safety step is to:

opts.text: Check the client's belongings for dangerous items and secure them per policy
opts.rat: Searching belongings for potential means of self-harm and securing them helps create a safe environment from the start.

opts.text: Leave all belongings with the client unchecked
opts.rat: Unchecked belongings may contain means of self-harm.

opts.text: Assume the client brought nothing dangerous
opts.rat: Assumptions are unsafe; belongings are checked per policy.

opts.text: Return any sharp items the client requests
opts.rat: Dangerous items are secured, not returned on request.

steps.q: When documenting a client's suicidal statement, the technician should:

opts.text: Record the statement in the client's exact words (in quotes) and the actions taken
opts.rat: Exact quotes and a record of the protective actions taken provide an accurate, useful account for the team.

opts.text: Write only a vague note that the client 'seemed upset'
opts.rat: Vague notes lose critical safety information; specifics and quotes are needed.

opts.text: Omit the statement to protect the client's image
opts.rat: Omitting a suicidal statement is unsafe and improper.

opts.text: Record a personal opinion that the client is faking
opts.rat: Documentation is objective; suicidal statements are taken seriously, not dismissed.

steps.q: During a shift, several clients need attention. Which should the technician prioritize FIRST?

opts.text: A client who just stated they intend to kill themselves now
opts.rat: An immediate, active expression of intent to die is a life-safety emergency that takes priority.

opts.text: A client asking for a snack
opts.rat: A routine request is lower priority than an active suicide statement.

opts.text: A client wanting to change the TV channel
opts.rat: This is a minor request, not a safety priority.

opts.text: A client requesting extra blankets
opts.rat: A comfort request is lower priority than an active safety emergency.

steps.q: When assessing a client's suicide risk, directly asking about a plan, method, and timing:

opts.text: Is appropriate and does NOT increase risk—it helps gauge how immediate and dangerous the risk is
opts.rat: Asking directly and specifically about plan, means, and timing is safe and essential for judging the level of risk.

opts.text: Will plant the idea and cause the client to attempt suicide
opts.rat: Asking directly does not create suicidal ideation; it opens the door to help.

opts.text: Should be avoided entirely
opts.rat: Direct, specific assessment is important, not something to avoid.

opts.text: Is only for the physician to ever discuss
opts.rat: Asking and reporting are within the technician's role, working with the team.

steps.q: A client with long-standing (chronic) suicidal thoughts now reports a NEW specific plan and has obtained a means. This represents:

opts.text: An acute escalation of risk requiring immediate protective action
opts.rat: A new plan and acquired means on top of chronic ideation signal acute escalation and call for immediate safety measures.

opts.text: No change, since the client always has these thoughts
opts.rat: A new plan and means are a significant escalation, not 'no change.'

opts.text: A reason to reduce observation
opts.rat: Escalation calls for increased, not reduced, protection.

opts.text: Something to address at the next scheduled meeting
opts.rat: Acute escalation requires immediate action, not delay.

steps.q: The technician suspects a client's suicidal statement is 'just for attention.' The correct approach is to:

opts.text: Take every suicidal statement seriously and assess and report it, regardless of perceived motive
opts.rat: All suicidal statements are treated seriously; dismissing one as attention-seeking can have fatal consequences.

opts.text: Ignore it because the client is 'seeking attention'
opts.rat: Ignoring a suicidal statement is dangerous; all are assessed and reported.

opts.text: Tell the client to stop being dramatic
opts.rat: This is dismissive, nontherapeutic, and unsafe.

opts.text: Wait to see if the client repeats it before acting
opts.rat: Statements are acted on promptly, not tested by waiting.

steps.q: Overall, the technician's role in suicide-safety care is to:

opts.text: Recognize risk and warning signs, maintain the ordered level of observation and a safe environment, respond immediately to escalation, and report and document accurately
opts.rat: The technician observes, keeps the client safe, acts on escalation, and reports/documents, working within the team's plan.

opts.text: Independently decide to discontinue suicide precautions
opts.rat: Changing precaution levels is a team/provider decision, not the technician's alone.

opts.text: Diagnose the client's disorder and prescribe treatment
opts.rat: Diagnosis and prescribing are outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Minimize or ignore suicidal statements
opts.rat: Suicidal statements are always taken seriously, never minimized.

reference:
Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Mental Health Care (suicide-risk care) — Phase-2 depth/application. Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level. Concepts are stated conceptually and marked for faculty confirmation: risk stratification (plan + available lethal means + prior attempt + imminent-risk behaviors), lethality assessment, means restriction (securing sharps, ligature risks, glass, bags, medications), matching observation level (continuous 1:1 with constant visual contact, including high-risk locations per policy), warning signs of imminent risk (giving away possessions, saying goodbye, sudden calm after despair), protective factors, the limits of 'no-suicide contracts' versus collaborative safety planning, priority physical care after an attempt, sustained risk post-attempt, elevated risk during transitions/discharge, belonging searches on admission, verbatim documentation, prioritization, that direct questioning does not increase risk, acute escalation of chronic ideation, and taking every statement seriously. Builds on and does not duplicate the foundational suicide items in mh-core-01. No specific statistics, doses, observation-interval minutes, or lab values are asserted. Pending faculty review.

If you or someone you know is in crisis, in the U.S. call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline). This resource note is for context and is not part of the exam item content.
